lead: A threat is only a possibility. It becomes a loss when it meets a weakness in something you own — an unpatched server, a reused password. This chapter gives each word its own job: asset, threat, threat agent, vulnerability, exposure, risk, attack vector, attack surface. It then shows how organisations keep these words in catalogs, leaning on the public lists CVE, CWE and CVSS, and how one number — risk, likelihood times impact — turns fear into a budget line. Every security purchase, from a patch project to a firewall, is argued with this arithmetic.
prereq: You need: 1.1 for the goals each risk is measured against, and 1.2 for the word 'attack'.

blocks.text: Four words carry most of the marks here. An asset is anything worth protecting: a server, a customer database, a login identity, the trust in a UPI app. A threat is a possible action that can damage an asset. The threat agent is who or what carries it out — a ransomware crew, a careless employee, a flood.

A vulnerability is the weakness that lets the threat succeed: an unpatched library, a blank admin password, an open S3 bucket. Without a vulnerability a threat stays imaginary. Without a threat a vulnerability stays harmless. Put them together and you get a threat–vulnerability pair — one sentence of the form 'this actor can use this weakness'. Exposure is how much sits open to that pair: 100 servers, one database, 4,000 accounts.

Risk is the expected size of the loss if the pair plays out. It is not the same as any of the three words above. A threat asks who acts, a vulnerability asks what is weak, and risk asks how much will this cost me per year.

An attack vector is the path the attacker uses to reach the weakness. The same weakness often has several vectors: an internet-facing SSH port is a remote vector, a USB stick dropped in the lobby is a physical vector, a phishing mail that steals the password is a human vector (see 1.6).

The attack surface is everything an attacker can reach at all: open ports, exposed APIs, employee mailboxes, third-party libraries, cloud storage buckets. Vector is a route; surface is the whole boundary of what is touchable.

Shrinking the surface is the cheapest defence: close unused ports, delete stale accounts, drop the library nobody imports. You cannot list vectors until you know the surface, which is why an asset inventory comes before everything else. Network-level vectors such as port scanning are in 1.4.

sections.h3: Catalogs: the lists an organisation keeps

blocks.text: Two living lists sit behind every risk register. The threat catalog records actors and their methods: ransomware crews, insider fraud, scripted scanning bots. The vulnerability catalog records known weaknesses in your own systems, each with an owner, the date found, the vector and the fix status. Both are updated on every scan, audit and incident.

items: CVE — Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures. One ID per specific flaw, written CVE-YYYY-NNNN. It names a flaw; it does not score it.
CWE — Common Weakness Enumeration. Groups flaws into classes such as buffer overflow or SQL injection, so you can fix a whole family at once.
CVSS — Common Vulnerability Scoring System. A severity score from 0 to 10, where 10 is the worst.

blocks.text: The working form of the catalog is the threat–vulnerability pair table: one row per sentence 'this actor can use this weakness', with columns for asset, threat agent, weakness, vector, current control and risk. Some syllabi call this compiling observations from organisational risk documents into a fixed table format, one column per field.
Risk exists so that a security argument can be checked. Two formulas cover the exam.

blocks.where: L is likelihood, the probability the pair succeeds within a stated period, as a fraction from 0 to 1. I is impact, the money lost if it does, in rupees. Risk is then in rupees per that period.

blocks.text: SLE = AV × EF,   ALE = SLE × ARO
blocks.where: AV is the asset value in rupees. EF is the exposure factor, the fraction of the asset destroyed per incident (0 to 1). SLE is the single loss expectancy, rupees per incident. ARO is the annualised rate of occurrence, incidents per year. ALE is the annualised loss expectancy, rupees per year.

blocks.text: A control is a change that lowers L, lowers I, or removes the vulnerability outright. Buy it when the drop in risk is bigger than its cost. That single comparison decides most security budgets.

examples.question: A firm runs 400 internal web servers. A scan finds that 25% of them use an unpatched library with a known remote-code-execution bug. The security team estimates the chance of a successful exploit in a year at 0.20. One successful exploit costs ₹50,00,000 in downtime, forensics and fines. (a) How many servers are exposed? (b) What is the annual risk in rupees? (c) A patch project costs ₹3,00,000 and cuts the yearly chance to 0.04. What is the new risk? (d) What is the net yearly saving?
steps: Exposed servers = fraction vulnerable × total servers = 0.25 × 400 = 100 servers.
Annual risk = likelihood × impact = 0.20 × ₹50,00,000 = ₹10,00,000 per year.
After the patch, likelihood becomes 0.04, so new risk = 0.04 × ₹50,00,000 = ₹2,00,000 per year.
Net saving = risk removed − control cost = ₹8,00,000 − ₹3,00,000 = ₹5,00,000 per year.
The saving is positive, so the patch project is worth funding on risk grounds alone.
examples.answer: 100 servers are exposed, the annual risk is ₹10,00,000, the patch cuts it to ₹2,00,000, and the net yearly saving is ₹5,00,000.
examples.check:
servers = 400
frac_vuln = 0.25
p_before = 0.20
p_after = 0.04
loss = 5000000
patch_cost = 300000
exposed = frac_vuln * servers
print(int(exposed))
risk_before = p_before * loss
print(int(risk_before))
risk_after = p_after * loss
print(int(risk_after))
saving = risk_before - risk_after - patch_cost
print(int(saving))

traps: Calling a vulnerability a threat, or a threat a risk. A threat is who or what can act; a vulnerability is the weakness that lets it work; risk is the expected damage, in rupees or in a severity score.
Treating CVE, CWE and CVSS as one thing. CVE identifies a single flaw, CWE names the class of weakness, CVSS gives a 0 to 10 severity. A CVE entry does not carry a score by itself.
Mixing up attack vector and attack surface. The vector is the route used for one attack; the surface is everything reachable, whether or not anyone is attacking today.
Writing likelihood as 20 instead of 0.20 in Risk = L × I, which inflates the answer by a factor of 100. L is a fraction; the impact carries the rupees.
Forgetting to subtract the control cost. A control that lowers risk is not automatically worth buying; only the saving net of its price counts.

quiz.q: Define threat agent and give two examples.
quiz.a: A threat agent is the person, group or event that can carry out a threat against an asset. Examples: a ransomware crew, a careless employee, a flood.

quiz.q: Why does a vulnerability cause no loss on its own?
quiz.a: A vulnerability is only a weakness. Loss needs an agent to reach it through some vector. With no threat agent, or with the weakness unreachable from any vector, the exposure never becomes an incident, so risk stays at zero.

quiz.q: A firm has 200 servers, 30% of them vulnerable. The yearly chance of a successful exploit is 0.10 and one exploit costs ₹20,00,000. Find the number of exposed servers and the annual risk.
quiz.a: Exposed = 0.30 × 200 = 60 servers. Annual risk = 0.10 × ₹20,00,000 = ₹2,00,000 per year.

quiz.q: Using the numbers in the previous question, a control costs ₹1,50,000 per year and cuts the chance of exploit to 0.02. Should the firm buy it?
quiz.a: New risk = 0.02 × ₹20,00,000 = ₹40,000. Risk removed = ₹2,00,000 − ₹40,000 = ₹1,60,000. Net saving = ₹1,60,000 − ₹1,50,000 = ₹10,000 per year. The saving is positive but thin, so the control is marginally worth buying and worth renegotiating on price.

quiz.q: What do the letters CVE, CWE and CVSS stand for, and what does each give you?
quiz.a: CVE is Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures, one ID per specific flaw. CWE is Common Weakness Enumeration, a class of weakness. CVSS is Common Vulnerability Scoring System, a severity score from 0 to 10.

quiz.q: Explain the difference between an attack vector and an attack surface with one example.
quiz.a: The attack surface is everything reachable: say, one web server with ports 80, 443 and 22 open plus an admin mailbox. The attack vector is the single route used for one attack, such as SSH password guessing on port 22. Closing port 22 shrinks the surface and removes that vector.

quiz.q: An asset is worth ₹80,00,000. One incident destroys 25% of it, and incidents happen twice a year. Find SLE and ALE.
Why keep a threat catalog of your own when CVE, CWE and CVSS are public and free?
quiz.a: The public lists describe flaws in general. They do not say which of your assets run the affected software, who your likely actors are, which vectors reach you, or who owns the fix. The local threat catalog and vulnerability catalog bind those public entries to your own assets, owners and deadlines, which is what a risk register needs.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry the pair table grows into a full risk register that auditors sample, and CVSS scores are combined with local context in schemes such as EPSS, which estimates the probability a flaw is exploited in the wild. Attack surface management is now a product category: tools continuously discover internet-facing assets nobody remembered creating, especially cloud buckets. Search next for 'CISA KEV catalog', which lists flaws known to be exploited, and for 'threat modelling with STRIDE', a method for listing threats before any scan runs. If you continue to Unit 6, risk management and audit show how these numbers become policy.
